explanations.explanation: Forty is right. The text says Joash "reigned in Jerusalem forty years." Joash is the king of Judah here, and forty years is a long run on any job. I've had oven mitts that didn't last half that.

Twenty sounds nice and round, but the text says forty. The temple trouble in this very passage is still going in the twenty-third year of his reign (2 Kings 12:6). So a twenty-year reign would be over before the story even gets going.

Twelve years would be a short stretch, but the text says forty. Joash is the king of Judah, and the temple repair problem alone runs past his twenty-third year (2 Kings 12:6). That's already almost double twelve, with a lot of reign still ahead.

True. The text says Joash "did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days he was instructed by Jehoiada the priest." Jehoiada is the priest who has been guiding him. A good teacher at your elbow is like a timer next to the oven: things come out better.

The text actually says Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days he was instructed by Jehoiada the priest. Jehoiada is the priest who was teaching him. So the right living and the instruction go together in this verse, and that makes the statement true.
Removed is the word. The text says, "Nevertheless, the high places were not removed." Joash did right, yet those places were still there. The people kept sacrificing and burning incense at them.

Close, but the verse says something else. It says the high places were not removed, and the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there. So "visited" undersells it. People were going there and using them, and nobody was dropping by for a quick look.

This one is a sneaky flip. If the high places were "not standing," they would be gone, and the text says the opposite. It says they were not removed. They were still there, and the people kept sacrificing and burning incense at them.

explanations.answer: All the money brought as sacred gifts
explanations.explanation: That's it. Joash tells the priests, "Collect all the money brought as sacred gifts into the house of the LORD." He names the census money, the money from vows, and the money brought voluntarily. So this is money people already gave for the house of the LORD.

explanations.answer: A new tax from every town in Judah
explanations.explanation: No new tax appears anywhere in this passage. Joash points to money already brought as sacred gifts into the house of the LORD. The census money, the money from vows, and the money brought voluntarily. Nobody had to go knocking on doors in every town.

explanations.answer: Silver from the priests' own homes
explanations.explanation: The priests' home savings never come up. Joash tells them to collect the money brought as sacred gifts into the house of the LORD. That's the census money, the money from vows, and the money brought voluntarily. Their own piggy banks were safe.
Right. Joash says the money "let it be used to repair any damage found in the temple." The money has one job. It's a short job description, and I respect that.
The guards don't get a mention here. Joash says the money is to be used "to repair any damage found in the temple." It's sacred gift money, and it has a temple-sized job to do.
No new palace in this plan. Joash says the money is for repairing any damage found in the temple. Nobody is sketching blueprints for a bigger house for the king.

Not quite. The text says that by the twenty-third year of Joash's reign, "the priests had not yet repaired the damage to the temple." So the work was still sitting there undone. That makes this statement false.

False is right. The text says that by the twenty-third year, the priests had not yet repaired the damage to the temple. That's a lot of years for one to-do item. I've seen dishes sit in the sink that long, and I'm not proud of it.

explanations.answer: Why they haven't repaired the temple
explanations.explanation: Yes. Joash asks, "Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple?" He gets right to it. Jehoiada the priest and the others are standing there, and the question is plain.

explanations.answer: Where all the census money went
explanations.explanation: The census money is one of the gifts Joash named earlier, but he doesn't ask where it went. His question is, "Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple?" The question is about the repairs not getting done.

explanations.answer: Who caused the damage to the temple
explanations.explanation: The text never says who caused the damage, and Joash doesn't ask. He asks, "Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple?" It's a question about the repair work. Jehoiada and the other priests are the ones he's asking.

explanations.answer: Take no more and hand it over
explanations.explanation: Yes. Joash says, "Now, therefore, take no more money from your constituency, but hand it over for the repair of the temple." The priests stop collecting from the people. The money they already have goes toward the repairs.

explanations.answer: Collect twice as much as before
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way. Joash says, "Now, therefore, take no more money from your constituency, but hand it over for the repair of the temple." The priests stop taking money from the people. Doubling it would have been a very different order.

explanations.answer: Store it in the royal palace
explanations.explanation: The palace isn't part of this order. Joash says to take no more money from the constituency and to hand it over for the repair of the temple. The money is headed to the temple repairs and not to the king's house.

Not this time. The text says the priests agreed they would not receive money from the people and "that they would not repair the temple themselves." So the repair work is no longer on their plate. This statement is false.

False is right. The priests agreed not to receive money from the people, and also "that they would not repair the temple themselves." The job moves to someone else. I bet they were relieved to put that one down.
Yes. Jehoiada set the chest "beside the altar on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD." Jehoiada is the priest who made it. The chest sits right where people walk in.
No gate of Sur here. The text says Jehoiada set the chest beside the altar, on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD. It's inside the house of the LORD.
The palace isn't where this chest goes. Jehoiada set it beside the altar, on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD. That's where the priests who guarded the threshold put the money.

explanations.answer: The royal scribe and the high priest
explanations.explanation: Right. When they saw a large amount of money in the chest, "the royal scribe and the high priest would go up, count the money." Then they tied it up in bags. A scribe and a high priest on the job. That's a counting crew.
Joash and his commanders aren't the counters here. The text says the royal scribe and the high priest would go up and count the money. Then they tied it up in bags.

The Carites don't show up in this passage. The counting is done by the royal scribe and the high priest, who go up when the chest holds a large amount. The priests who guarded the threshold are the ones who put the money in.

Yes. The supervisors paid those doing the work: "the carpenters, builders, masons, and stonecutters." That's the crew actually fixing the house of the LORD. The money went to the people with the tools.
Singers and gatekeepers aren't on this payroll. The supervisors paid the carpenters, builders, masons, and stonecutters. That's the crew doing the repair work.
No soldiers on this list. The supervisors paid the carpenters, builders, masons, and stonecutters. Trumpets come up in a moment as something the money did not buy (2 Kings 12:13).
True. The text says they "purchased timber and dressed stone to repair the damage to the house of the LORD." They also paid the other expenses of the repairs. All of it was aimed at the repair work.

The text says otherwise. They "purchased timber and dressed stone to repair the damage to the house of the LORD," and they paid the other expenses of the temple repairs. So the chest money did buy those materials. That makes the statement true.

Close, but the text says the opposite. The money was not used for making silver basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, trumpets, or any articles of gold or silver. Those would be nice things, but that's not what this money was for. So the statement is false.

False is right. The text says the money "was not used for making silver basins, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, trumpets, or any articles of gold or silver." It went to the workers who repaired the house of the LORD. Shiny extras had to wait.

Yes. The text says no accounting was required from the men who received the money, "because they acted with integrity." That's the reason the text gives. Honest people can handle money without anybody hovering over them.
Jehoiada is the priest who set up the chest, but the text doesn't say he vouched for anyone. It gives one reason: they acted with integrity. That's why no accounting was required.

explanations.answer: Because the king ordered it so
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say the king ordered it. It gives a different reason: the men who paid the workers acted with integrity. That's why no accounting was required from them.

Yes. The text says the money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings "was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests." So it stayed separate from the repair money in the chest.
The poor aren't named here. The text says the money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD, and that it belonged to the priests.
Joash doesn't get this money. The text says the money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD. It belonged to the priests.

explanations.answer: He sends Hazael the sacred objects
explanations.explanation: Right. Joash "took all the sacred objects dedicated by his fathers" and sent them to Hazael. Hazael is the king of Aram, who had captured Gath and decided to attack Jerusalem. The text says that after Joash sent them, Hazael withdrew.

explanations.answer: He marches out to fight Hazael
explanations.explanation: Joash doesn't march out in this passage. Hazael, king of Aram, had captured Gath and decided to attack Jerusalem. Joash gathered sacred objects and gold and sent them to Hazael instead.

explanations.answer: He hides in the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: No hiding is mentioned. Hazael, king of Aram, had decided to attack Jerusalem. What Joash did was gather the sacred objects and gold and send them to Hazael.

Gold is right. Joash sent Hazael "all the gold found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace." He also sent the sacred objects from Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, the kings of Judah he calls his fathers, plus his own consecrated items. That was a big load to send.

Bronze isn't on the list. The text says Joash sent all the gold found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace. He sent it along with the sacred objects and his own consecrated items.

No weapons in this shipment. The text says Joash sent all the gold found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace. He sent it along with the sacred objects and his own consecrated items.
True. The text says, "So Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem." Hazael, king of Aram, had decided to attack, but he pulled back after Joash sent the gifts.
The text says otherwise. After Joash sent the sacred objects and gold, "Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem." So he did pull back. That makes the statement true.
That's right. The text says, "the servants of Joash rose up and formed a conspiracy and killed him." This is a heavy part of the story. It happened at Beth-millo, on the road down to Silla.

Gath comes up earlier, when Hazael captured it. But the conspiracy against Joash came from his own servants. The text says they rose up, formed a conspiracy, and killed him. This is a heavy part of the story.
The priests of Baal aren't in this passage. The text says the servants of Joash rose up and formed a conspiracy against him. It's a heavy ending to his story.

explanations.answer: With his fathers in the City of David
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says, "they buried him with his fathers in the City of David." Joash was laid to rest among the kings before him. His story closes quietly.

explanations.answer: In his mother's town of Beersheba
explanations.explanation: Beersheba is where his mother Zibiah was from (2 Kings 12:1). It's not where he's buried. The text says they buried him with his fathers in the City of David.
Beth-millo, on the road down to Silla, is where he was struck down. It's not where he was buried. The text says they buried him with his fathers in the City of David.
Amaziah is right. The text says, "his son Amaziah reigned in his place." The crown stays in the family. The story of Judah's kings keeps rolling.
Hezekiah isn't named in this passage. The text says Joash's son Amaziah reigned in his place.
Jehoram is one of the kings of Judah that Joash calls his fathers (2 Kings 12:18), so he came before Joash. The son who reigned in his place was Amaziah.
